passages.text: LIVER, in anatomy, the largest gland of the body, of a dark red colour, situated in the right side of the belly under the diaphragm.
Its office is to separate the bile from the blood, which is brought to it chiefly by the vena portae, a vein that collects the blood from the stomach, intestines, and spleen.
The bile is collected in the gall-bladder, and passes by the common duct into the intestine, where it assists in the digestion of the food.

The ancients, following Galen, believed the liver to be the workshop of the blood, in which the chyle was changed into blood; but this opinion has been given up since the discovery of the lacteal vessels and of the circulation.
The ancients also placed in the liver the seat of love and of the passions; whence the poets speak of a wounded liver.
If the liver be much wounded, the wound is commonly mortal; nor is it known that any part of it, once destroyed, is ever restored.
The liver is a large organ found in vertebrates. In humans it lies in the upper right part of the abdomen, below the diaphragm. It is the largest gland in the human body.
The liver produces bile, which helps the body digest fats. Bile is stored in the gallbladder and released into the small intestine.
The liver gets blood from two sources. The hepatic portal vein brings blood from the digestive tract and the spleen, and the hepatic artery brings oxygen-rich blood.
The liver stores glucose as glycogen and releases it when the body needs it. Claude Bernard described this role of the liver in the 1850s.
The liver makes many blood proteins, including albumin and clotting factors. It also breaks down toxic substances such as alcohol and many drugs.
The liver can regenerate. After part of it is removed or damaged, the remaining tissue can grow back to about its former size.
In many ancient cultures the liver was seen as a seat of life or of the emotions. In Greek myth an eagle ate the liver of Prometheus each day, and it grew back each night.
In the early months of fetal life the liver is a main site of blood cell production. The bone marrow takes over this role before birth.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: bile, gall-bladder, portal vein, diaphragm.
Bile scores well but covers only one of the liver's tasks.

alignments.label: Largest gland

britannica.quote: the largest gland of the body

wikipedia.quote: the largest gland in the human body

alignments.note: Same fact, almost the same words.

alignments.label: Making bile

britannica.quote: Its office is to separate the bile from the blood

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Liver cells make bile. The 1797 entry also gives the liver only this one office.

alignments.label: Portal vein

britannica.quote: brought to it chiefly by the vena portae

wikipedia.quote: The hepatic portal vein brings blood from the digestive tract and the spleen

alignments.note: Same vein in new words. Wikipedia adds the hepatic artery as a second supply.

alignments.label: Gall-bladder and digestion

britannica.quote: The bile is collected in the gall-bladder

wikipedia.quote: Bile is stored in the gallbladder

alignments.note: Same fact. Wikipedia names fats as the food that bile helps to digest.

alignments.label: Liver and blood making

britannica.quote: this opinion has been given up

wikipedia.quote: the liver is a main site of blood cell production

alignments.note: The 1797 entry rejects Galen, and this holds for the adult. Inference: the fetal liver does make blood cells, so the rejection is too broad.

alignments.label: Seat of the passions

britannica.quote: placed in the liver the seat of love and of the passions

wikipedia.quote: seen as a seat of life or of the emotions

alignments.note: Both report the old belief. Neither endorses it.

alignments.label: Regrowth

britannica.quote: nor is it known that any part of it, once destroyed, is ever restored

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. The liver can grow back after part of it is lost.

alignments.label: Glycogen store
alignments.note: Claude Bernard found this role in the 1850s, after the 1797 edition.

alignments.label: Proteins and toxins

wikipedia.quote: breaks down toxic substances such as alcohol and many drugs

alignments.note: The 1797 entry does not mention protein making or the breakdown of poisons.
